etymology: The New Testament office of overseer and shepherd of the local church; from the Greek presbyteros, “elder,” equivalent to episkopos, overseer, and poimēn, pastor.
biblical_def: An elder is the New Testament officer charged to oversee, teach, and shepherd the local church—the same office named by three interchangeable terms: elder (presbyter), bishop (overseer), and pastor (shepherd), all denoting one office, not three ranks. The dictionary holds, with the Reformed and Baptist confessions, that Christ has appointed two offices in His church, elder and deacon, and that the eldership is the office of rule and teaching. The work is good and to be desired: if a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work. The qualifications are chiefly of character: a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach—a man whose life adorns the doctrine he proclaims. Elders rule and they feed: they that rule well are counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine; and the flock is charged, obey them that have the rule over you, for they watch for your souls as they that must give account. The dictionary reads the elder as Christ’s undershepherd—a qualified man, set apart to teach the Word, guard the doctrine, rule with gentleness, and feed the flock—not a lord over God’s heritage but a servant who will give account to the Chief Shepherd for the souls committed to his care.
webster_summary: The New Testament office of overseer, teacher, and shepherd of the local church; one office under three terms—elder, bishop, pastor—to rule well and feed the flock.

corruption_summary: The office is corrupted by a hierarchy of ranks Rome built upon it, by women’s ordination against the qualifications, and by lordly rule; Scripture knows one office of qualified men who shepherd, not lord.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Several corruptions touch the office. Rome and the prelatical churches built upon the single New Testament office a graded hierarchy of priests, bishops, archbishops, and pope, dividing what Scripture joins, for elder, bishop, and pastor name one office, not three ranks. The modern church, against the plain qualification that an elder be the husband of one wife and the apostolic order that forbids a woman to teach or usurp authority over the man, has opened the office to women in defiance of the Word. And in every age the temptation is to rule as a lord over God’s heritage rather than as a servant of the flock.

The principle to recover is the elder as Christ’s undershepherd, qualified by character and charged to feed the flock. The office is one, held by men who meet the apostolic qualifications—blameless, sober, apt to teach, ruling their own houses well—set apart to teach the Word, guard the doctrine, and shepherd the souls of the church. They rule, and the flock submits; but they rule not as lords but as servants who watch for souls and must give account to the Chief Shepherd. The eldership is a good work to be desired, a sacred trust to be filled by faithful men, and a stewardship for which every elder will answer at the appearing of Christ.
roots_summary: The New Testament office of overseer, teacher, and shepherd of the church; one office under three terms—elder, bishop, pastor—to rule well and feed the flock.

etymology: The New Testament pattern of more than one elder shepherding each local church; from the Latin pluralitas, a plurality.
biblical_def: Plurality of elders is the New Testament pattern by which each local church is shepherded not by a single solitary minister but by a plurality—a team of qualified elders ruling and feeding the flock together. The pattern is consistent across the apostolic records. Paul and Barnabas ordained elders—plural—in every church; Paul called for the elders—plural—of the one church at Ephesus; he wrote to the saints at Philippi with the bishops—plural—and deacons; James bids the sick call for the elders—plural—of the church. Nowhere does the New Testament present a lone pastor ruling a congregation by himself. The wisdom of this pattern is plain: a plurality guards against the unchecked authority and the isolation of one man, provides mutual accountability and counsel, spreads the burden of oversight, and embodies the truth that the flock belongs to Christ and not to any single shepherd. The dictionary reads plurality of elders as the biblical and healthy ordering of the local church—a council of qualified men sharing the rule, mutually accountable, laboring together to feed and guard the flock—a safeguard against both the tyranny of one man and the disorder of no leadership, and a reflection of the shared, servant character of Christ’s undershepherds.
webster_summary: The New Testament pattern of a team of elders shepherding each local church together, guarding against the unchecked rule of one man and embodying shared, accountable oversight.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the solitary-pastor model and, oppositely, the rule of a celebrity senior pastor both depart from the New Testament plurality of accountable elders.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The departures to name lie on two sides. On one side is the solitary-pastor model, common in much of evangelicalism, where a single minister bears the whole weight of rule without fellow elders to share it—a man isolated, unaccountable, and overburdened, a pattern the New Testament nowhere presents. On the other side is the modern celebrity-pastor church, where a dominant senior figure reduces any other elders to a rubber stamp, concentrating in one man an authority Scripture spreads among a plurality. Both depart from the apostolic order, and both have borne bitter fruit in the unchecked falls and the wounded flocks of recent memory.

The principle to recover is the shared, accountable oversight of a plurality of elders. The apostles ordained elders in every church and addressed the elders of each congregation in the plural; the flock belongs to Christ, and He shepherds it through a team of qualified men, not a solitary ruler. This plurality provides mutual accountability and counsel, guards against the tyranny and isolation of one man, spreads the burden of oversight, and reflects the servant character of Christ’s undershepherds, who rule together under the Chief Shepherd. The healthy church is led by elders who watch over one another even as they watch over the flock.

etymology: A congregation meeting in a private home, as in the New Testament era; the church gathered in a household.
biblical_def: A house church is a congregation gathered for worship in a private home, the ordinary form in which the earliest churches met before the age of dedicated buildings. The New Testament repeatedly greets the church that meets in a house: the church in the house of Aquila and Priscilla, the church in the house of Nymphas, the church in Philemon’s house. The first believers continued daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart. The dictionary observes that the church is never the building but always the people—the called-out assembly of Christ—and that a true church may gather in a home, a hall, or a hired room as well as a steeple-house; what makes a church is not the place but the marks: the Word truly preached, the sacraments rightly administered, and discipline duly exercised under qualified elders. House churches have flourished in times of persecution, when believers met in secret as the early Christians did, and continue today where the gathered church has no building. Yet the dictionary cautions that the home setting does not excuse a church from the biblical order: it still needs ordained elders, the faithful preaching of the Word, the ordinances, and accountable structure. The dictionary reads the house church as a legitimate and ancient form of the gathered church—the people of God assembled in a home—valid wherever the marks of a true church are present, and a witness that the church is the worshipping people, not the walls.
webster_summary: A congregation gathered for worship in a private home, the ordinary form of the earliest churches; valid wherever the marks of a true church are present, for the church is the people, not the building.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the house-church label is sometimes used to escape the biblical order of elders, ordinances, and discipline; the home setting does not excuse a church from being a true church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The caution to name is the misuse of the house-church idea to escape the biblical order of the church. Some, weary of structure, gather informally in homes while dispensing with ordained elders, the faithful preaching of the Word, the ordinances rightly administered, and the discipline that marks a true church—mistaking informality for purity. But the home setting changes only the place, not the requirements. A church in a house is still a church, owing the same submission to the Word: it needs qualified elders, the preaching of the gospel, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, and accountable order. A casual gathering that lacks the marks of a true church is not a purer church but a defective one.

The principle to recover is that the church is the worshipping people, not the building, yet ordered by the Word wherever it meets. The earliest churches met in homes and the gathered people of God may rightly do so still, especially under persecution; what makes a true church is not the place but the marks—the Word truly preached, the sacraments rightly administered, discipline duly exercised. The house church is a legitimate and ancient form of the assembly, valid wherever those marks are present, and a standing witness that Christ’s church is the called-out people, gathered around His Word and table, whether in a home or a hall.

etymology: The brotherhood and mutual discipleship of Christian men; from the Latin fraternitas, brotherhood.
biblical_def: Men’s fraternity is the brotherhood and mutual discipleship of Christian men—the gathering of brothers to sharpen, encourage, and build one another up in the faith and in the manful duties God lays upon them. Scripture commends such brotherly sharpening: iron sharpeneth iron, so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend; two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labour. It charges men to a holy manliness: watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong; and to the passing on of sound doctrine from man to man, committing the things heard to faithful men who shall be able to teach others also. The dictionary commends the gathering of Christian men for prayer, the study of the Word, accountability, and the strengthening of one another for their callings as husbands, fathers, churchmen, and workers—a needed labor in an age that has confused and softened biblical manhood. Yet it guards two boundaries: such fraternity is no substitute for the gathered church under its elders, nor a license to import the worldly bravado of mere masculinity untethered from the cross. The dictionary reads men’s fraternity as the wholesome brotherhood of Christian men who sharpen one another by the Word—quitting themselves like men, bearing one another’s burdens, and provoking one another to love and good works—under the authority of Scripture and within the life of the church.
webster_summary: The brotherhood and mutual discipleship of Christian men, sharpening one another in the faith and in their callings; a wholesome labor under the Word and within the life of the church.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though men’s ministry can drift into worldly bravado or replace the church; true fraternity sharpens men by the Word under the church’s authority.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two drifts attend men’s ministry. The first is the importing of worldly masculinity—mere bravado, competitiveness, and a tribal toughness—untethered from the cross, so that the gathering forms men in the image of the age rather than of Christ. The second is the tendency to let a parachurch fraternity, however good, drift into a substitute for the gathered church, with its own loyalty replacing membership, accountability, and the ordinances under ordained elders. Biblical manhood is not the world’s machismo, and no band of brothers, however earnest, is the church.

The principle to recover is brotherly sharpening under the Word and within the church. Christian men are to sharpen one another as iron sharpens iron, to quit themselves like men and stand fast in the faith, to bear one another’s burdens and commit sound doctrine to faithful men. Such fraternity is a wholesome and needed labor, especially in an age that has confused manhood; but it serves the church, it does not replace her, and it forms men by the cross, not by the world’s bravado. Men sharpened by the Word in true brotherhood return strengthened to their callings as husbands, fathers, churchmen, and workers, to the glory of God.

etymology: The joint service of a husband and wife in the work of the gospel, as Aquila and Priscilla; ministry shared within the marriage bond.
biblical_def: Couple ministry is the joint service of a husband and wife in the work of the gospel—the two who are one flesh laboring together for Christ, as heirs together of the grace of life. The chief biblical example is Aquila and Priscilla, the tentmaking couple who were Paul’s helpers in Christ Jesus, who hosted a church in their house, and who together took the eloquent Apollos and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly. Their partnership shows the strength of a believing marriage poured out in service: hospitality, instruction, the risking of their own necks for Paul, the building up of the church—done together. Scripture teaches that the husband and wife are heirs together of the grace of life, and that two are better than one, a threefold cord not quickly broken. The dictionary commends such joint ministry while keeping it within the biblical order it everywhere honors: the husband and wife serve as complementary partners, the wife a true fellow-laborer, yet the order of headship is not erased, and the public office of teaching and ruling in the gathered church remains with qualified men—Priscilla instructed Apollos privately, alongside her husband, not as an ordained teacher over the assembly. The dictionary reads couple ministry as the fruitful labor of a believing husband and wife together for the gospel—a threefold cord of the two and the Lord—exercised in hospitality, discipleship, and service, within the creational order and to the building up of Christ’s church.
webster_summary: The joint service of a believing husband and wife for the gospel, as Aquila and Priscilla; fruitful partnership within the creational order, the wife a true fellow-laborer alongside her husband.

corruption_summary: Couple ministry is misused to erase the order of headship and to install women in the office of teaching and ruling the church; rightly kept, it is fruitful partnership within the creational order.
corruption_paragraphs: The misuse to name is the pressing of couple ministry, and of Priscilla’s example, into an argument against the biblical order—as though her instructing of Apollos overturned the apostolic word that a woman is not to teach or usurp authority over the man in the church, and as though joint ministry meant the erasing of headship and the installing of wives in the office of elder. But Priscilla and Aquila instructed Apollos privately, together, in their home—not in the public assembly, and not as an ordained teacher ruling the congregation. The complementarian order the dictionary everywhere honors is not abolished by a believing wife’s true and valuable labor; the two truths stand together.

The principle to recover is fruitful partnership within the creational order. The believing husband and wife are heirs together of the grace of life, a threefold cord with the Lord not quickly broken, and their joint labor in hospitality, discipleship, and service is a great strength to the church, as Aquila and Priscilla’s was to Paul. The wife is a true fellow-laborer, honored and valued, her gifts employed; yet the husband’s headship is not erased, and the public office of teaching and ruling the gathered church remains with qualified men. Couple ministry honors both the partnership and the order, and is the more fruitful for keeping them together.

etymology: The support of gospel ministry by one’s own labor, after the example of Paul, who made tents; bivocational ministry.
biblical_def: Tentmaking is the support of gospel ministry by the minister’s own labor with his hands, after the example of the apostle Paul, who, being of the same craft as Aquila, abode with him and wrought, for by their occupation they were tentmakers. Paul labored night and day at his trade that he might not be chargeable to the churches and might offer the gospel without cost, even though he taught plainly that the Lord had ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel, and that the laborer is worthy of his hire. Paul did not deny the right of ministers to be supported by the church—he defended it—but for the sake of the gospel and to stop the mouths of those who would accuse him of preaching for gain, he often waived that right and worked, neither eating any man’s bread for nought but laboring that he might be an example. The dictionary reads tentmaking as the honorable practice of self-supporting, bivocational ministry, exemplified by Paul: a lawful and sometimes wise course, especially in pioneer fields, in poor or new churches, and where support would hinder the gospel or expose the minister to slander. It holds together two truths the Word keeps together—that the church ought to support those who labor in the Word, and that a minister may, for the gospel’s sake, support himself by his own hands—and commends the tentmaker who labors that the gospel may go forth free and unhindered.
webster_summary: Self-supporting, bivocational ministry after the example of Paul, who made tents that he might preach without charge; lawful and often wise, though the church ought to support those who labor in the Word.

corruption_summary: Tentmaking is misused to deny ministers their rightful support, or despised as second-rate ministry; Scripture holds both truths—the right to support and the freedom to work—as Paul did.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two errors touch the practice. The first uses Paul’s tentmaking to deny ministers their rightful support, as though a faithful pastor ought always to work a trade and never be paid by the church—against the plain word that the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel, and that the elders who labor in the Word are worthy of double honour. The second despises tentmaking as a second-rate or unspiritual ministry, looking down on the bivocational pastor as a lesser laborer—forgetting that the greatest of the apostles worked with his hands. Both miss the balance Scripture keeps.

The principle to recover is the holding together of two truths, as Paul held them. The church ought to support those who labor in the Word; the laborer is worthy of his hire, and Paul defended that right plainly. Yet a minister may, for the gospel’s sake, waive that right and support himself by his own labor—as Paul did, that he might preach without charge, stop the mouths of slanderers, and be an example to the idle. Tentmaking is honorable and often wise, especially in pioneer fields and poor or new churches; the tentmaker labors that the gospel may go forth free, and the supported pastor receives his due that he may give himself wholly to the Word.

etymology: The carrying of the gospel to the nations beyond Israel; from the Latin gentilis, of the nations, and missio, a sending.
biblical_def: The Gentile mission is the carrying of the gospel beyond Israel to the nations of the world—the great outward movement of redemption from the one chosen people to all the families of the earth. It was promised from the first: in Abraham’s seed all nations would be blessed; the suffering Servant would be a light to the Gentiles, for salvation to the ends of the earth. The risen Lord commanded it: go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. At Pentecost the Spirit was poured out, and through Peter at the house of Cornelius and supremely through Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles, the door of faith was opened to the nations. The mystery long hidden was now revealed: that the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of God’s promise in Christ by the gospel—not by becoming Jews, but by faith in Christ, the middle wall of partition broken down. The dictionary reads the Gentile mission as the fulfillment of God’s ancient purpose to gather a people from every nation—the gospel breaking the bounds of Israel to reach the world, the church becoming the one new man of Jew and Gentile in Christ, and the Great Commission driving the people of God to the ends of the earth until a multitude out of every nation, kindred, tongue, and people stands before the throne.
webster_summary: The carrying of the gospel beyond Israel to the nations; promised to Abraham, commanded in the Great Commission, and advanced through Paul, the apostle of the Gentiles.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the exclusivity of the gospel is denied and missions recast as cultural imperialism; the Gentile mission is God’s purpose to save a people from every nation through Christ alone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The errors to name are two. The first is the pluralism that denies the necessity of the Gentile mission—holding that the nations are already saved in their own religions and need not hear of Christ, so that missions becomes mere dialogue or aid rather than the proclamation of the only name under heaven whereby men must be saved. The second is the charge that missions is cultural imperialism, the West imposing its religion on the world—a charge that forgets the gospel is no Western possession but God’s good news for every nation, and that it has been received and carried by believers of every tongue. Both would silence the command to teach all nations.

The principle to recover is the Gentile mission as the fulfillment of God’s ancient purpose. From the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed in his seed, to the Servant set as a light to the Gentiles, to the risen Lord’s command to disciple all nations, God has purposed to gather a people from every nation, kindred, tongue, and people. The Gentiles are saved not by becoming Jews but by faith in Christ, fellowheirs in the one new man, the middle wall broken down. The church’s task until He comes is the Great Commission—to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth, that the multitude no man can number may stand at last before the throne.

etymology: The offering gathered by the churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor saints at Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8–9; Romans 15).
biblical_def: The Macedonian collection is the great offering Paul gathered among the Gentile churches—chiefly Macedonia and Achaia—for the relief of the poor saints at Jerusalem, and the occasion of the fullest teaching on Christian giving in the New Testament. Paul holds up the churches of Macedonia as a marvel of grace: in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality; they gave beyond their power, of their own accord, first giving their own selves to the Lord. From their example he draws the principles of gospel giving: that it flows from grace and from Christ’s own self-giving—though He was rich, yet for our sakes He became poor; that it is to be purposed in the heart, not grudgingly nor of necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver; that he which soweth bountifully shall reap bountifully; and that the collection both relieved the poor and bound Jew and Gentile together in the one body. The dictionary reads the Macedonian collection as the pattern of Christian liberality: giving born of grace, modeled on the poverty Christ embraced for us, offered cheerfully and sacrificially out of even deep poverty, purposed in the heart, and serving both the relief of the needy and the unity of the church—a witness that grace received overflows in grace given.
webster_summary: The offering Paul gathered among the Gentile churches for the poor saints at Jerusalem; the New Testament’s fullest pattern of cheerful, sacrificial, grace-born Christian giving.

It relieved the poor and bound Jew and Gentile in one body (Rom 15:26).
scriptures: Moreover, brethren, we do you to wit of the grace of God bestowed on the churches of Macedonia;

corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel twists “sow bountifully, reap bountifully” into a scheme to enrich the giver; the Macedonian collection is grace-born, cheerful, sacrificial giving for the relief of the poor and the unity of the church.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The misuse to name is the prosperity gospel’s perversion of Paul’s teaching on the collection—ripping “he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully” from its context to promise the giver a financial return, so that giving becomes an investment to enrich oneself. But the Macedonian churches gave out of deep poverty, not for gain but out of grace, first giving their own selves to the Lord; and the harvest Paul promises is the increase of righteousness and thanksgiving to God, not a swollen bank account. To make Christian giving a transaction for personal wealth is to turn the grace of liberality into the greed it opposes.

The principle to recover is grace-born, cheerful, sacrificial giving. The collection’s pattern is plain: giving flows from the grace of God and from Christ’s own self-giving, who though He was rich became poor for our sakes; it is purposed in the heart, not grudging nor of compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver; it may be sacrificial even out of deep poverty, as in Macedonia; and it serves both the relief of the needy and the binding together of the church, Jew and Gentile in one body. Grace received overflows in grace given; the Macedonian collection is the abiding model of how the people of God open their hands to one another.

etymology: The church as the household and family of God, His adopted children and one another’s brethren; from the biblical figures of household, sonship, and brotherhood.
biblical_def: The family of God is one of the great figures Scripture uses for the church—the household of God, His adopted children, brothers and sisters of one another and of Christ the elder Brother. Believers are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God; the church is the house of God, the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth. By adoption the redeemed are made sons: behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God. And being children of one Father, they are brethren one to another, charged to do good especially unto them who are of the household of faith. This family is not founded on flesh and blood but on the new birth and adoption in Christ; its bond is thicker than natural kinship, for the Lord said that whosoever does the will of His Father is His brother and sister and mother. The dictionary reads the family of God as the church in her warmth and nearness—the redeemed gathered into one household under one Father, made sons by adoption, brethren to one another, bound by a love and loyalty that the natural family only foreshadows—so that the lonely are set in families, the orphaned given a Father, and the believer brought into a people who are nearer than brothers, the household of God for ever.

corruption_summary: The family of God is sentimentalized into mere belonging without holiness, or set against the natural family; rightly held, it is the household founded on the new birth, binding the redeemed in love and duty.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two distortions touch the figure. The first sentimentalizes the family of God into mere belonging and acceptance without holiness—a warm fellowship that asks nothing of repentance, faith, or obedience, as though one were born into God’s family by good feeling rather than by the new birth and adoption in Christ. The second sets the family of God against the natural family, as if devotion to the church relieved one of the God-given duties to spouse, children, and parents. But Scripture honors both: the man who provides not for his own house has denied the faith, even as the church is the household of God.

The principle to recover is the family of God founded on the new birth and binding the redeemed in love and duty. The church is a true family—the household of God, His adopted sons, brethren of one another and of Christ—but a family entered not by flesh and blood nor by mere belonging, but by regeneration and adoption through faith in Christ. Its bond is real and weighty: believers are to do good especially to the household of faith, to bear one another’s burdens, to love as brethren. This family does not abolish the natural one but fulfills and outlasts it, gathering the lonely into a people and giving the orphaned a Father who will never leave them.

etymology: The covenant bond of brotherly love among the members of Christ’s church; from the biblical “brotherhood” and the covenant of mutual love and watchfulness.
biblical_def: The brotherhood covenant is the bond of brotherly love and mutual duty that joins the members of Christ’s church one to another—the covenant, whether formally written or simply lived, by which believers commit to love, watch over, bear with, and build up one another as brethren. Scripture names the church a brotherhood and commands its love: love the brotherhood; let brotherly love continue. The Lord gave it as His new commandment: that ye love one another, as I have loved you, that ye also love one another—and by this all men shall know we are His disciples. The psalmist sang its sweetness: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Many churches express this bond in a church covenant—a solemn agreement of members to walk together in love, to watch over one another, to attend the worship and ordinances, to submit to discipline, and to seek one another’s good—giving formal shape to the mutual obligations the New Testament everywhere assumes. The dictionary reads the brotherhood covenant as the committed, covenantal love of church members for one another: not a loose and optional friendliness, but a binding fellowship of brethren who have given themselves to the Lord and to one another, to love, watch over, and build up the body in unity, until they dwell together for ever in the household of God.
webster_summary: The covenant bond of brotherly love and mutual duty joining the members of Christ’s church; committed, watchful love—often formalized in a church covenant—not a loose friendliness.

scriptures: Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.

corruption_summary: Church membership is reduced to a loose, optional friendliness with no real bond or accountability; the brotherhood covenant is the committed, watchful love the New Testament assumes among brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the reduction of church fellowship to a loose, consumer-style friendliness—believers attending when convenient, committing to no one, accountable to no one, treating the church as a service to be sampled rather than a brotherhood to be joined. In this drift the rich New Testament language of loving the brotherhood and watching over one another is hollowed out, and the church becomes a crowd of strangers who happen to share a building. But the Scripture knows no such uncommitted Christianity; it everywhere assumes a real, binding fellowship of brethren who belong to one another in the Lord.

The principle to recover is the committed, covenantal love of church members. The brotherhood is to be loved, brotherly love to continue, the new commandment kept—that we love one another as Christ loved us; and how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Many churches give this formal shape in a church covenant, a solemn mutual agreement to walk together in love, to watch over one another, to attend the worship and ordinances, and to submit to loving discipline. Whether written or lived, the bond is real: brethren who have given themselves to the Lord and to one another, to love, bear with, and build up the body, until they dwell together for ever in the family of God.
